<!-- introtheorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-all-good}
Let $\mathcal{O}_K$ be the valuation ring of a finite extension $K/\mathds{Q}_p$, and let $\mathscr X\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ be a smooth proper morphism of algebraic spaces with projective generic fibre $Y$ whose base change $Y_{\overline K}$ is a hyperk\"ahler variety of dimension $2n\ge4$.
For the special fibre $X$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $X$ is quasi-$F$-split;
\item $X$ is Frobenius split;
\item $\operatorname{H}^2_{\operatorname{crys}}(X/W)[1/p]$ has a nonzero slope-zero part.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $\operatorname{ht}(X)\in\{1,\infty\}$.
<!-- end introtheorem-1 -->
<!-- introtheorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-family}
A primitive symplectic variety $Z$ of dimension $2n\ge4$ over a perfect field is quasi-$F$-split if and only if it is Frobenius split; in particular $\operatorname{ht}(Z)\in\{1,\infty\}$.
Moreover the Hodge-good locus is open in any smooth proper family with geometrically connected fibres of dimension $2n\ge4$ and trivial relative canonical sheaf, so the dichotomy holds near any Hodge-good fibre.
<!-- end introtheorem-2 -->
<!-- introtheorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:deformation type of hilbert and kummer}
Let $n\ge2$, and let $X/k$ be a smooth proper variety Hodge-deformation equivalent to either
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $S^{[n]}$ for a $K3$ surface $S/k$, with $p>n$; or
\item $K_n(A)$ for an abelian surface $A/k$, with $p>n+1$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $X$ is primitive symplectic, its Hodge--de Rham spectral sequence degenerates at $E_1$, and $\operatorname{H}^j_{\operatorname{crys}}(X/W)$ is torsion-free for every $j$.
Its mixed-characteristic formal deformations are unobstructed; in particular, $X$ admits a smooth proper formal lifting over $W$ and a smooth proper lifting over $W_2$.
For every $1\le i\le n$, the Artin--Mazur functor $\Phi_X^{2i}$ is prorepresentable by a smooth one-dimensional formal group over $k$, and
\[
  X\text{ is quasi-}F\text{-split}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\text{ is }F\text{-split}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{ht}(\Phi_X^2)=1.
\]
If $p>2n$, the Hodge-deformation hypothesis may be replaced by a finite chain of smooth proper families joining $X$ to the same standard model, over smooth connected finite-type bases, for which $b\mapsto h^2(\mathcal{Y}_b,T_{\mathcal{Y}_b})$ is locally constant on closed points (condition \eqref{eq:ct2}).
<!-- end introtheorem-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:f-split}
$X$ is \emph{$F$-split} if the natural map $\mathcal{O}_X \to F_* \mathcal{O}_X$ splits as a morphism of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:Fsplit}
Let $Z$ be a smooth proper geometrically connected algebraic space of dimension $d$ with $\omega_Z\simeq\mathcal{O}_Z$ over a field $k$ of characteristic $p$ that is $F$-finite, that is $[k:k^p]<\infty$.
Then $Z$ is Frobenius split if and only if the absolute Frobenius acts nontrivially on $\operatorname{H}^d(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The $F$-finiteness of $k$ makes the absolute Frobenius of $Z$ finite.
Grothendieck and Serre duality for proper algebraic spaces \cite[Tags~0E58 and~0E61]{stacks-project} identify the restriction map
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_Z}(F_*\mathcal{O}_Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)\longrightarrow
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_Z}(\mathcal{O}_Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)=k
\]
with the dual of Frobenius on $\operatorname{H}^d(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)$; here the dualizing complex is $\omega_Z[d]$.
The map $\mathcal{O}_Z\toF_*\mathcal{O}_Z$ splits precisely when $1\ink$ has a preimage under this restriction map.
Since its target is one-dimensional, this is equivalent to the map, and hence Frobenius on $\operatorname{H}^d(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)$, being nonzero.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:quasi-f-split}
$X$ is \emph{$n$-quasi-$F$-split} if $\Phi_{X,n}$ admits an $\mathcal{O}_X$-linear retraction.
The \emph{quasi-$F$-split height} (or \emph{Yobuko height}) is
\[
  \operatorname{ht}(X) \;=\; \min\{\, n \ge 1 \mid X \text{ is } n\text{-quasi-}F\text{-split} \,\}
  \;\in\; \mathds{Z}_{\ge 1} \cup \{\infty\},
\]
with $\operatorname{ht}(X)=\infty$ if no such $n$ exists; $X$ is \emph{quasi-$F$-split} if $\operatorname{ht}(X)<\infty$.
\footnote{The same invariant is denoted $h_F(X)$ elsewhere in the literature.}
In particular, $X$ is $F$-split if and only if $\operatorname{ht}(X)=1$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:basic-properties}
Let $X$ be a smooth proper algebraic space over $k$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $X$ is $n$-quasi-$F$-split then it is $(n+1)$-quasi-$F$-split; in particular $F$-split $\Rightarrow$ quasi-$F$-split.
\item If $X$ is quasi-$F$-split, then $\operatorname{H}^j(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)\coloneqq\varprojlim_r \operatorname{H}^j(X,W_r\mathcal{O}_X)$ is a finitely generated $W$-module for every $j$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
(1) A retraction $\sigma$ of $\Phi_{X,n}$ gives a retraction $\sigma\circ R$ of $\Phi_{X,n+1}$, since $R\circ\Phi_{X,n+1}=\Phi_{X,n}$; the case $n=1$ gives the last assertion.

(2) For schemes this is \cite[Theorem~1.2]{Nakkajima2022}; we follow its proof on the \'etale site to extend it to algebraic spaces.
Let $B_{r}\Omega^1_{X}$ be the cokernel of $F\colonW_r\mathcal{O}_X\to F_*W_r\mathcal{O}_X$.
The Cartier operator and the pushout defining $Q_{X,r}$ give exact sequences
\[
\begin{aligned}
  0&\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow Q_{X,r}
    \longrightarrowB_{r}\Omega^1_{X}\longrightarrow0,\\
  0&\longrightarrow F_*B_{r-1}\Omega^1_{X}\longrightarrow Q_{X,r}
    \longrightarrow F_*\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow0\qquad(r\ge2).
\end{aligned}
\]
They hold on $X$ because they can be checked on \'etale scheme charts.
For $h=\operatorname{ht}(X)<\infty$, the first sequence splits when $r\ge h$ by (1); the second then gives
\[
  \dim_k\operatorname{H}^j(X,B_{r}\Omega^1_{X})
  \le\dim_k\operatorname{H}^j(X,B_{r-1}\Omega^1_{X})
  \qquad(r\ge\max\{h,2\}).
\]
Thus these dimensions are bounded.
Finite-level Witt cohomology has finite length and satisfies the Mittag--Leffler condition \cite[Proposition~4.5.2]{Olsson2007Crystalline}.
Serre's finite-generation criterion \cite[arXiv version~2, Remark~4.5]{Nakkajima2022}, applied to the inverse limit of $\operatorname{H}^j(X,B_{r}\Omega^1_{X})$, now yields the claim.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:F-finite}
The criterion of \Cref{lem:Fsplit}, the definition of \Cref{def:quasi-f-split}, and the implication in \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(1) apply over any $F$-finite field, without assuming perfection.
Every residue field of a scheme of finite type over the perfect field $k$ is $F$-finite.
The Witt-cohomology and Cartier-module results below are stated over perfect fields, for which $W(k)$ is a complete discrete valuation ring.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:petrov-degeneration}
If $X$ is quasi-$F$-split, then the Hodge--de Rham spectral sequence degenerates at the first page.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This is \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Petrov2025}, which gives a decomposition of the de Rham complex of a quasi-$F$-split smooth proper variety.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:quasi F split is W2 litable}
Let $X$ be a smooth proper geometrically connected variety over $k$ with $\omega_{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}_X$.
If $X$ is quasi-$F$-split, then $X$ is $W_2(k)$-liftable.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By \Cref{lem:petrov-degeneration}, quasi-$F$-splitting makes the Hodge--de Rham spectral sequence degenerate at $E_1$.
For a smooth proper geometrically connected variety with trivial canonical bundle, this implies $W_2(k)$-liftability by \cite[Theorem~7.18]{BrantnerTaelman2025}.
The input is \cite[Theorem~1.3]{AchingerSuh2023}: for $d=\dim X$, the conjugate differential
\[
  d_2^{d-2,1}\colon\operatorname{H}^{d-2}(X^{(p)},\Omega^1_{X^{(p)}/k})
  \longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^d(X^{(p)},\mathcal{O}_{X^{(p)}})
\]
is cup product with the obstruction to lifting $X^{(p)}$, and Serre duality with a volume form equates their vanishing.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:artin-mazur}
For $q\ge1$, the \emph{Artin--Mazur functor} of $X$ in degree $q$ is
\[
  \Phi^q_X\colon\mathrm{Art}_k\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Ab}),
  \qquad
  \Phi^q_X(A)=\ker\bigl(\operatorname{H}^q_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_A,\mathds{G}_m)\longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^q_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathds{G}_m)\bigr),
\]
the kernel of restriction to the closed fibre \cite[\S II]{ArtinMazur1977}.
For $q=1$ this is the formal Picard functor $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}_X$, and for $q=2$ the formal Brauer functor $\widehat{\mathrm{Br}}_X$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:AM-prorepresentable}
Let $X$ be a smooth proper algebraic space over $k$ of dimension $d$, and let $q\ge1$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item The tangent space of $\Phi^q_X$ is $\operatorname{H}^q(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$, and obstructions to lifting along a square-zero extension in $\mathrm{Art}_k$ lie in $\operatorname{H}^{q+1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
\item If $\operatorname{H}^{q-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$, then $\Phi^q_X$ is prorepresentable.
\item If in addition $\operatorname{H}^{q+1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$, which is automatic for $q=d$, then $\Phi^q_X$ is formally smooth; if moreover $\dim_k\operatorname{H}^q(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=1$, then $\Phi^q_X$ is a smooth one-dimensional formal group.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
These are the criteria of \cite[\S II, Corollaries~2.4--2.5 and 4.2--4.4]{ArtinMazur1977}.
The proofs apply on the \'etale site of a proper algebraic space: nilpotent thickenings preserve the \'etale topos, coherent cohomology is finite-dimensional, and smoothness gives vanishing above degree $d$.
For (1), a square-zero extension $A\twoheadrightarrow A/I$ in $\mathrm{Art}_k$ gives the exact sequence
\[
  1\longrightarrow 1+I\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{X_A}^{\times}
   \longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{X_{A/I}}^{\times}\longrightarrow1,
  \qquad 1+I\mathcal{O}_X\simeq I\otimes_k\mathcal{O}_X ,
\]
Its cohomology sequence identifies the kernel of $\Phi^q_X(A)\to\Phi^q_X(A/I)$ as a quotient of $I\otimes_k\operatorname{H}^q(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ and places the obstruction to surjectivity in $I\otimes_k\operatorname{H}^{q+1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
Taking $A=k[\varepsilon]$ gives the tangent space; for $q=d$ the obstruction group vanishes by cohomological dimension.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:AM-cartier}
If $\Phi^q_X$ is prorepresentable, there is a canonical isomorphism of Cartier modules
\[
  \mathbf{M}(\Phi^q_X)\;\simeq\;\operatorname{H}^q(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)
  \coloneqq\varprojlim_r\operatorname{H}^q(X,W_r\mathcal{O}_X).
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This is \cite[\S II, Corollary~4.3]{ArtinMazur1977}; see \cite[Proposition~6.3.3]{MondalReinecke2026} for a modern account.
The computation uses the multiplicative formal group and the Witt sheaves on the \'etale site, so it applies equally to smooth proper algebraic spaces.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:AM-slope-convention}
If $\Phi^q_X$ is a smooth one-dimensional formal group of finite height $h$, then $(D_q)_{[0,1)}$ is isoclinic of slope $1-\tfrac1h$ and dimension $h$; if its height is infinite, then $(D_q)_{[0,1)}=0$ (\Cref{prop:AM-cartier,prop:WittSlope}).
Here Frobenius is the crystalline Frobenius acting on the covariant Cartier module $\operatorname{H}^q(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:yobuko-height}
Let $X$ be a Calabi--Yau variety of dimension $d\ge2$ over $k$, that is, smooth proper with $\omega_X\simeq\mathcal{O}_X$ and $\operatorname{H}^i(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ for $0<i<d$.
Then $\Phi^d_X$ is a smooth one-dimensional formal group and
\[
  \operatorname{ht}(X)=\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^d_X).
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The hypotheses give $\operatorname{H}^{d-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$, and Serre duality together with $\omega_X\simeq\mathcal{O}_X$ gives $\operatorname{H}^d(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\simeq\operatorname{H}^0(X,\mathcal{O}_X)^\vee=k$, so $\Phi^d_X$ is a smooth one-dimensional formal group by \Cref{lem:AM-prorepresentable}.
The equality of heights is \cite[Theorem~4.5]{YobukoQuasiFSplit}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:nakkajima-inequality}
Let $X$ be a smooth proper variety over $k$, and let $q\ge1$.
Assume that $\Phi^q_X$ is prorepresentable, that
\[
  \operatorname{H}^q(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=k,\qquad \operatorname{H}^{q+1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0,
\]
and that the Bockstein maps $\beta_m\colon\operatorname{H}^{q-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\to\operatorname{H}^q(X,W_{m-1}\mathcal{O}_X)$ vanish for every $m\ge2$.
Then
\[
  \operatorname{ht}(\Phi^q_X)\;\le\;\operatorname{ht}(X).
\]
In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^q_X)=\infty$ forces $\operatorname{ht}(X)=\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This is \cite[Theorem~1.5]{Nakkajima2022}, applied to $X$ with the trivial log structure, which is log smooth of Cartier type over $k$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:AM-infinite-height}
If $\Phi^q_X$ is prorepresentable by a smooth one-dimensional formal group of infinite height, its Cartier module $\operatorname{H}^q(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is not finitely generated over $W$ (\Cref{prop:AM-cartier}).
Thus $X$ is not quasi-$F$-split by \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(2), without any Bockstein vanishing hypothesis.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:AM-recent}
Without the vanishing in \Cref{lem:AM-prorepresentable}(2), the criterion gives no automatic prorepresentability of the classical Artin--Mazur functor.
For this reason, \Cref{def:crystalline-height} defines the degree-two invariant using crystalline cohomology.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:good-reduction}
We say $X_K$ has \emph{good reduction} at $\mathfrak{p}$ if there is a smooth proper morphism of algebraic spaces $\mathcal{X} \to \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}$ with generic fibre $\mathcal{X}_K \cong X_K$.
The \emph{reduction} associated with this model is the special fibre
\[
  X \;=\; \mathcal{X} \times_{\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}} k ,
  \qquad k=\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak p,
\]
a smooth proper algebraic space over $k$ of dimension $2n$.
The total space $\mathcal{X}$ is regular; neither $\mathcal{X}$ nor $X$ is required to be a scheme or to be projective over its base.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:k3}
A $K3$ surface is a hyperk\"ahler variety of dimension $2$, and its good reduction is again a $K3$ surface.
Higher-dimensional examples include Hilbert schemes of points on $K3$ surfaces and generalised Kummer varieties; we return to their reductions in \Cref{ex:hilb,ex:kummer}.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:canonical-good}
In the setting above, $X$ is geometrically connected and geometrically integral, and
\[
  \omega_X\simeq\mathcal{O}_X,\qquad\chi(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=n+1 .
\]
The same assertions hold after any finite extension of the residue field.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The number of geometric connected components is locally constant in a smooth proper family of algebraic spaces \cite[Tag~0E1E]{stacks-project}; hence $X$ is geometrically connected, and smoothness makes it geometrically integral.
Hilbert's Theorem 90 descends the trivialisation of $\omega_{Y_{\overline K}}$ to $Y$.
Viewed as a rational section of $\omega_{\mathscr X/\mathcal{O}_K}$, it has divisor $aX$ for some $a\in\mathds{Z}$, since $X$ is the only vertical prime divisor.
The divisor $X$ is principal, cut out by a uniformiser, so rescaling gives a nowhere-vanishing relative canonical section and hence $\omega_X\simeq\mathcal{O}_X$; the divisor argument is checked on \'etale charts of $\mathscr X$.
Finally, proper flat cohomology and base change give a perfect complex for the two fibres \cite[Tag~0CTM]{stacks-project}, so $\chi(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=\chi(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)=n+1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:automatic-picard}
After extension to an algebraic closure of the residue field, every good reduction $X$ satisfies
\[
  \pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X)=1,\qquad \operatorname{Alb}_{X/k}=0,\qquad
  (\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/k})_{\mathrm{red}}=0 .
\]
Moreover, the absolute Frobenius acts nilpotently on $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Work over an algebraic closure of $k$.
After passing to a complete strictly henselian trait, finite \'etale covers of $X$ extend to the proper model; a connected cover has geometrically connected generic fibre by smooth proper constancy.
Thus $\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{\overline K})\twoheadrightarrow\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X)$, and the source is trivial.
The Albanese variety is therefore zero, since a nonzero abelian variety has a nonzero prime-to-$p$ Tate module detected by $\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X)$; its dual $(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{X/k})_{\mathrm{red}}$ is zero as well.

Put $V=\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
The Artin--Schreier sequence gives $\ker(F-1\colon V\to V)=\operatorname{H}^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathds{F}_p)=0$.
The bijective part of a $p$-semilinear operator over an algebraically closed field has fixed vectors by Lang's theorem, so it must vanish here.
Hence $F$ is nilpotent on $V$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:h1-not-automatic}
The vanishing $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ is \emph{not} a formal consequence of \Cref{prop:automatic-picard}: a finite connected Picard scheme in characteristic $p$ may have nonzero tangent space while its reduced subscheme is a point.
This is why the dichotomy below is proved through crystalline slopes rather than through the coherent cohomology algebra.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:h1-vanishing-small-e}
Let $X$ be a good reduction of a hyperk\"ahler variety as above.
Suppose the absolute ramification index of $K$ is at most $p-1$.
Then $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
After a faithfully flat base change we may assume that $k$ is algebraically closed.
This preserves the absolute ramification index of $K$ and the desired vanishing of coherent cohomology descends along the base change.
Let $P^{\tau} = \operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}_{\mathscr X/\mathcal{O}_K}$.
Since $\mathscr{X}/\mathcal{O}_K$ is smooth proper with geometrically connected fibres, it is cohomologically flat in degree $0$.
Hence $P^{\tau}$ is an algebraic space of finite type whose formation commutes with base change.
Since the fibers of $\mathscr{X}/\mathcal{O}_K$ are geometrically normal, $P^{\tau}$ is separated and equidimensional over $\mathcal{O}_K$ \cite[Theorem~3.6(i),(iii)]{FringuelliViviani2023}.

Let $S = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ and $z\colon S\to P^{\tau}$ be the zero section.
Raynaud's Picard-flatness theorem \cite[Theorem~4.1.2]{Raynaud1979Picard}, in the algebraic-stack formulation of \cite[Theorem~8.1(ii)]{FringuelliViviani2023}, implies that $P^{\tau}$ is flat along $z$ whenever the absolute ramification index is at most $p-1$.
Thus there is a Zariski open neighbourhood $U$ of $z(S)$ in $P^{\tau}$ such that $U\to S$ is flat.
The generic fibre of $P^{\tau}$ is trivial, since it is the $\tau$-part of the Picard scheme of a hyperk\"ahler variety in characteristic zero; hence $U_K=z(K)$.
Since $P^{\tau}$ is separated over $S$, $z(S)$ is closed in $U$.
Its ideal sheaf vanishes on $U_K$, and therefore vanishes on $U$ by flatness over the discrete valuation ring.
Consequently $U=z(S)$, so $z(k)$ is an open reduced point of $P^{\tau}_k$ and
\[
  \operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X) = \mathrm{T}_{z(k)} P^{\tau}_k = 0. \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:WA}
Let $Q$ be a weakly admissible filtered $\varphi$-module with $\operatorname{Fil}^0Q_K=\operatorname{Fil}^1Q_K=Q_K$.
Then every Newton slope of $Q$ is at least $1$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose the slope subisocrystal $Q_{<1}$ spanned by the slopes below one were nonzero.
It is $\varphi$-stable, and we give it the induced filtration.
Since $\operatorname{Fil}^1Q_K=Q_K$, the induced filtration on $(Q_{<1})_K$ also satisfies $\operatorname{Fil}^1=(Q_{<1})_K$, whence $t_H(Q_{<1})\ge\dim Q_{<1}$.
On the other hand every Newton slope of $Q_{<1}$ is strictly less than $1$, so $t_N(Q_{<1})<\dim Q_{<1}$.
This contradicts the weak-admissibility inequality $t_H(Q_{<1})\le t_N(Q_{<1})$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:automatic-D2-block}
For every good reduction, exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,
  beginpenalty=10000,midpenalty=10000]
  \item $(D_2)_{[0,1)}=0$; or
  \item there is a unique integer $h\ge1$ for which $(D_2)_{[0,1)}$ is isoclinic of slope $1-\tfrac1h$ and has dimension $h$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The filtered $\varphi$-module $D_2$ is weakly admissible with effective Hodge weights $0,1,2$ and $\dim\operatorname{gr}^0(D_2)_K=h^{0,2}(Y)=1$.
Put $S=(D_2)_{[0,1)}$ for simplicity.
Let $r=\dim S$.
The induced filtration on $S_K$ embeds $\operatorname{gr}^a S_K$ into $\operatorname{gr}^a(D_2)_K$ for every $a$.
In particular $\operatorname{gr}^0S_K$ is at most one-dimensional.
Since the filtration is effective, we have
\[
  t_H(S)\ \ge\ 0\cdot\dim\operatorname{gr}^0S_K+1\cdot\bigl(r-\dim\operatorname{gr}^0S_K\bigr)\ \ge\ r-1 .
\]
Weak admissibility gives $t_H(S)\le t_N(S)$, whence
\[
  \delta(S)=r-t_N(S)\le1 .
\]
Slopes of $D_2$ are all non-negative: the sum $N$ of the negative slope subspaces is $\varphi$-stable with $t_H(N)\ge0$ by effectivity and $t_N(N)<0$ if $N\ne0$, which would contradict $t_H(N)\le t_N(N)$.

Let $\lambda = a/b$ be a slope of $S$ in lowest terms with $0 \leq a <b$.
By Dieudonn\'e--Manin theory its multiplicity is divisible by $b$, and an isoclinic part of multiplicity $mb$ contributes the positive integer $m(b-a)$ to $\delta(S)$.
Hence, if $S\ne0$, the bound $\delta(S)\le1$ forces exactly one part to occur.
This part necessarily has multiplicity $b$ and $b-a=1$; taking $h=b$ gives \textup{(ii)}, together with its uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:crystalline-height}
For a good reduction $X$, define its \emph{degree-two crystalline height} by
\[
  h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X):=
  \begin{cases}
    \dim_{K_0}(D_2)_{[0,1)}, & \text{if }(D_2)_{[0,1)}\ne0,\\
    \infty, & \text{if }(D_2)_{[0,1)}=0.
  \end{cases}
\]
By \Cref{prop:automatic-D2-block}, every finite value is a positive integer $h$, and $(D_2)_{[0,1)}$ is then isoclinic of slope $1-\tfrac1h$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:ordinary-surface-slopes}
Let $Z$ be a $K3$ surface or an abelian surface over a perfect field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$. Then $Z$ is ordinary if and only if $D_2(Z)$ has a nonzero slope-zero part. In this case $(D_2(Z))_{[0,1)}$ is a line of slope zero, and the slopes of $D_2(Z)$ are $0,1,2$, with multiplicities $1,20,1$ in the $K3$ case and $1,4,1$ in the abelian case.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Both types of surfaces have torsion-free crystalline cohomology and trivial canonical bundle, so $h^{0,2}(Z)=h^{2,0}(Z)=1$. If $Z$ is ordinary, its degree-two Newton and Hodge polygons agree \cite[Proposition~7.3]{BlochKato1986}, giving the stated slope multiplicities.

Conversely, for a $K3$ surface the formal Brauer group is smooth and one-dimensional, so \Cref{rem:AM-slope-convention} shows that a nonzero slope-zero part is equivalent to height one, hence to ordinarity. For an abelian surface $A$, the exterior-algebra description $D_2(A)\simeq\bigwedge^2D_1(A)$ gives slope-zero multiplicity $\binom{f(A)}{2}$, where $f(A)$ is the $p$-rank. This is nonzero exactly when $f(A)=2$, that is, when $A$ is ordinary.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:hilb}
Let $\mathscr S\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ be smooth and proper with $K3$ generic fibre and special fibre $S/k$, and let $X=S^{[n]}$ be the good reduction of the Hilbert scheme $\operatorname{Hilb}^n$ of the generic fibre, a hyperk\"ahler variety of dimension $2n\ge4$.
For the Mukai vector $v=(1,0,1-n)$, the degree-two isomorphism \cite[Proposition~4.4(iii)]{FuLi2021} gives a decomposition of $F$-isocrystals
\[
  D_2(X)\simeq D_2(S)\oplusK_0(-1).
\]
The last summand comes from the exceptional divisor, so $(D_2(X))_{[0,1)}\simeq(D_2(S))_{[0,1)}$.
Thus $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$ if and only if $S$ is ordinary, by \Cref{lem:ordinary-surface-slopes} and \eqref{eq:iii-equiv}.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:kummer}
Let $\mathscr A/\mathcal{O}_K$ be an abelian scheme with special fibre $A/k$, and suppose that the relative generalised Kummer variety $\mathscr X=K_n(\mathscr A)$ is smooth and proper over $\mathcal{O}_K$; this holds, for example, if $p\nmid n+1$ \cite[Proposition~6.5]{FuLi2021}.
Set $X=K_n(A)$, of dimension $2n\ge4$.
The degree-two calculation in \cite[proof of Proposition~6.7]{FuLi2021} and the exterior-algebra description of abelian cohomology give
\[
  D_2(X)\simeq D_2(A)\oplusK_0(-1)
  \simeq \bigwedge^2D_1(A)\oplusK_0(-1)
\]
as $F$-isocrystals. Hence $(D_2(X))_{[0,1)}\simeq(D_2(A))_{[0,1)}$, and $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$ if and only if $A$ is ordinary, by \Cref{lem:ordinary-surface-slopes} and \eqref{eq:iii-equiv}.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:quotient}
For $1\le i\le n$, cup product gives an injective morphism of isocrystals
\[
  \operatorname{Sym}^i D_2\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow D_{2i},
\]
whose cokernel $Q_i$ has all Newton slopes at least $1$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:less1iso}
  (D_{2i})_{[0,1)}\simeq(\operatorname{Sym}^i D_2)_{[0,1)} .
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Verbitsky's theorem gives an injection $\operatorname{Sym}^i\operatorname{H}^2(Y_{\mathds{C}},\mathds{Q})\hookrightarrow\operatorname{H}^{2i}(Y_{\mathds{C}},\mathds{Q})$ for $i\le n$ \cite{Verbitsky1996,Bogomolov1996}; its image is the Verbitsky component, and the injectivity of the corresponding map in the Betti, $\ell$-adic and potentially semistable $p$-adic realisations is recorded in \cite[Theorem~3.14]{IIKTZ2025}.
For $Y$ over an arbitrary field of characteristic zero the statement follows by spreading out and choosing an embedding of a finitely generated field of definition into $\mathds{C}$.

The de Rham cup map is therefore injective, and the $B_{\mathrm{dR}}$-comparison yields an injective $G_K$-equivariant map $\operatorname{Sym}^i V_2\hookrightarrow V_{2i}$, where $V_m=\operatorname{H}^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_{\overline K},\mathds{Q}_p)$; let $U_i$ denote its cokernel.
The category of crystalline representations is closed under subquotients, and $D_{\operatorname{crys}}$ is exact and compatible with tensor operations, so $U_i$ is crystalline and $D_{\operatorname{crys}}(U_i)=Q_i=D_{2i}/\operatorname{Sym}^iD_2$.
In particular $Q_i$ is weakly admissible.

Morphisms of weakly admissible filtered $\varphi$-modules are strict, so on degree-zero graded pieces the cup map becomes $\operatorname{Sym}^i\operatorname{H}^2(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)\to\operatorname{H}^{2i}(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)$.
For an irreducible hyperk\"ahler variety both sides are one-dimensional and this map is an isomorphism; hence $\operatorname{gr}^0(Q_i)_K=0$, and effectivity gives $\operatorname{Fil}^1(Q_i)_K=(Q_i)_K$.
By \Cref{lem:WA}, every Newton slope of $Q_i$ is at least one.
Finally, slope truncation is exact for isocrystals (as one checks after extending the perfect residue field, using Dieudonn\'e--Manin), so applying the interval $[0,1)$ to the exact sequence
\[
  0\to\operatorname{Sym}^iD_2\to D_{2i}\to Q_i\to 0
\]
yields \eqref{eq:less1iso}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:automatic-top-slopes}
Every good reduction $X$ of dimension $2n\ge4$ satisfies
\[
  \dim_{K_0}(D_{2n})_{[0,1)}=
  \begin{cases}
    1, & h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1,\\
    0, & h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1,
  \end{cases}
\]
and in the first case $(D_{2n})_{[0,1)}$ is a line of slope zero.
Equivalently, $\operatorname{H}^{2n}_{\operatorname{crys}}(X/W)[1/p]$ has a nonzero slope-zero part if and only if $\operatorname{H}^2_{\operatorname{crys}}(X/W)[1/p]$ does.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:less1iso} the left-hand side is $(\operatorname{Sym}^nD_2)_{[0,1)}$, and the slopes of $\operatorname{Sym}^nD_2$ are the sums of $n$ slopes of $D_2$.
If $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}=1$, the unique slope of $D_2$ below one is a slope-zero line and all other slopes are at least one; the $n$-th power of that line is then the unique summand of $\operatorname{Sym}^nD_2$ with slope below one, and it is again a slope-zero line.
If $1<h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}<\infty$, the smallest slope of $D_2$ is
\[
  1-\tfrac{1}{h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}}\ge\tfrac{1}{2}
\]
so every slope of $\operatorname{Sym}^nD_2$ is at least $\tfrac n2\ge1$.
If $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}=\infty$ the assertion is immediate.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:WittSlope}
For every smooth proper algebraic space $X/k$ and every $q$ there is a Frobenius-compatible isomorphism
\[
  \operatorname{H}^q(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)\otimes_WK_0\simeq (D_q)_{[0,1)} .
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
This is the $r=0$ case of the rational slope spectral sequence \cite[\S II, Corollary~3.5]{Illusie1979}.
For algebraic spaces, use the de Rham--Witt comparison and slope spectral sequence on the \'etale site \cite[Theorems~4.4.17 and~4.5.15]{Olsson2007Crystalline}; the degree-zero term is $W\mathcal{O}_X$, with the same Frobenius convention.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:hodge-good}
Let $X$ be a smooth proper algebraic space over $k$ of even dimension $2n$.
We say that $X$ is \emph{Hodge-good} if there is a class $\eta\in\operatorname{H}^2(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ for which cup product induces an isomorphism of graded $k$-algebras
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HG}
  \operatorname{H}^\bullet(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\;\simeq\;k[\eta]/(\eta^{n+1}),
  \qquad\deg\eta=2 .
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $\operatorname{H}^{2i}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=k\,\eta^i$ for $0\le i\le n$ and $\operatorname{H}^j(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ for every odd $j$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:hodge-good-reduction}
A \emph{Hodge-good reduction} is a good reduction in the sense of \Cref{def:good-reduction} which is Hodge-good in the sense of \Cref{def:hodge-good}.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:HG-not-automatic}
After shrinking the base of a fixed arithmetic spread of a hyperk\"ahler variety, coherent cohomology commutes with base change and the cup-power maps are isomorphisms, so the fibres are Hodge-good.
This does not establish Hodge-goodness at every good reduction: both the dimensions of coherent cohomology and the nonvanishing of cup powers require justification at an arbitrary good prime.
The dichotomy of \Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy} is therefore proved without this hypothesis.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:AM-hodge-good}
Let $X$ be a Hodge-good smooth proper algebraic space of dimension $2n$ over $k$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item For every even $q=2i$ with $1\le i\le n$, the functor $\Phi^{2i}_X$ is prorepresentable and formally smooth with tangent space $\operatorname{H}^{2i}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=k\,\eta^i$; hence it is a smooth one-dimensional formal group.
\item For every odd $q$ with $1\le q\le 2n-1$, the functor $\Phi^q_X$ is zero.
  In particular no odd formal group enters the height argument.
\item If $X$ is a Hodge-good reduction of a hyperk\"ahler variety, then $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_X)=h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
(1) By \eqref{eq:HG} we have $\operatorname{H}^{2i-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=\operatorname{H}^{2i+1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$, the second also for $i=n$ by cohomological dimension, and $\dim_k\operatorname{H}^{2i}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=1$; now apply \Cref{lem:AM-prorepresentable}.

(2) For a square-zero extension $A\twoheadrightarrow A/I$ in $\mathrm{Art}_k$ the sequence displayed in the proof of \Cref{lem:AM-prorepresentable} exhibits $\ker\bigl(\Phi^q_X(A)\to\Phi^q_X(A/I)\bigr)$ as a quotient of $I\otimes_k\operatorname{H}^q(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$, which vanishes for odd $q$.
Induction along the powers of the maximal ideal of $A$ gives $\Phi^q_X(A)=0$.

(3) By (1) and \Cref{rem:AM-slope-convention}, $(D_2)_{[0,1)}$ is isoclinic of slope $1-1/\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_X)$ and of dimension $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_X)$ when the height is finite, and is zero when it is infinite.
Comparing with \Cref{prop:automatic-D2-block} and \Cref{def:crystalline-height} gives the equality.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:boxcup}
For $a,b\ge1$ with $a+b\le n$, the cup product of Witt-vector cohomology induces a canonical morphism of formal Lie groups
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mubox}
  \mu_{a,b}\colon E_a\boxtimes E_b\longrightarrow E_{a+b},
\end{equation}
and $\mu_{a,b}$ is an isomorphism.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:boxpowers}
  \Phi^{2i}_X\;\simeq\;(\Phi^2_X)^{\boxtimes i}\qquad(1\le i\le n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The products of the Witt sheaves give a continuous $W$-balanced pairing $M_a\times M_b\to M_{a+b}$, $(x,y)\mapsto x\smile y$, subject to the standard Witt identities
\[
  F(x\smile y)=Fx\smile Fy,\qquad
  V(x\smile Fy)=Vx\smile y,\qquad
  V(Fx\smile y)=x\smile Vy .
\]
These are exactly the $(V,F)$-bilinearity relations of \cite[Definition~4.7 and Example~4.8]{AntieauNikolaus2021}; such pairings are corepresented by the Cartier box product \cite[Lemma~4.9]{AntieauNikolaus2021}, and the construction passes to derived $V$-completion \cite[Proposition~4.14]{AntieauNikolaus2021}.
As $M_{a+b}$ is $V$-complete we obtain $M_a\mathbin{\widehat\boxtimes}_{W}M_b\to M_{a+b}$, which by the covariance of $\mathbf{M}$ and \eqref{eq:boxCartier} is a morphism in the direction \eqref{eq:mubox}.

It remains to compute the differential of $\mu_{a,b}$.
Cartier theory gives $\operatorname{Lie}(E_i)\simeq M_i/VM_i$ \cite[Theorem~4.23]{Zink1984}.
The exact sequences
\[
  0\longrightarrowW_{r-1}\mathcal{O}_X\xrightarrow{\ V\ }W_r\mathcal{O}_X
   \xrightarrow{\ R_{r-1}\ }\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow0
\]
together with $\operatorname{H}^{2i-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ show that $V$ is injective on $M_{i}$.
Then, passing to the limit along the restriction maps, the uniqueness of $V$-preimages gives $\ker\bigl(M_i\to\operatorname{H}^{2i}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\bigr)=VM_i$ and hence an injection
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhoi}
  \rho_i\colon M_i/VM_i\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^{2i}(X,\mathcal{O}_X).
\end{equation}
Both sides are one-dimensional, the left by \Cref{prop:AM-hodge-good}(1) and the right by \eqref{eq:HG}, so $\rho_i$ is an isomorphism.
Reduction modulo $V$ is symmetric monoidal \cite[Lemma~4.12 and Proposition~4.14]{AntieauNikolaus2021}, whence
\[
  \operatorname{Lie}(E_a\boxtimes E_b)\simeq(M_a/VM_a)\otimes_k(M_b/VM_b),
\]
and since $R_{r-1}\colonW\mathcal{O}_X\to\mathcal{O}_X$ is a map of sheaves of rings, the differential of $\mu_{a,b}$ is identified under \eqref{eq:rhoi} with the ordinary cup product
\[
  \operatorname{H}^{2a}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\otimes_k\operatorname{H}^{2b}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\longrightarrow
  \operatorname{H}^{2a+2b}(X,\mathcal{O}_X),
\]
which sends $\eta^a\otimes\eta^b$ to $\eta^{a+b}\ne0$ and is therefore an isomorphism.
The source of \eqref{eq:mubox} is again a smooth one-dimensional formal Lie group \cite[Proposition~7.2.17]{MondalReinecke2026}, and a morphism of smooth one-dimensional formal schemes with invertible differential is an isomorphism by the formal inverse function theorem\cite[discussion after Definition~1.22]{Zink1984}.
Iterating \eqref{eq:mubox} gives \eqref{eq:boxpowers}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:boxheights}
Let $X$ be a Hodge-good smooth proper algebraic space of dimension $2n\ge4$ over $k$ and write $h=\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_X)$, which equals $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)$ if $X$ is a Hodge-good reduction.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:heightpattern}
  \bigl(\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_X),\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^4_X),\dots,\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^{2n}_X)\bigr)=
  \begin{cases}
    (1,1,\dots,1), & h=1,\\
    (h,\infty,\dots,\infty), & 1<h<\infty,\\
    (\infty,\infty,\dots,\infty), & h=\infty .
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Heights may be computed after extending $k$ to an algebraic closure.
If $h=1$, then $E_1\simeq\widehat{\mathds{G}}_m$, which is the unit for $\boxtimes$ \cite[Remark~7.2.20]{MondalReinecke2026}; by \eqref{eq:boxpowers} every $E_i$ is then of height one.
If $h>1$, possibly infinite, then the box product of two one-dimensional formal Lie groups of height greater than one is $\widehat{\mathds{G}}_a$ \cite[Proposition~7.2.21]{MondalReinecke2026}, so $E_2\simeq E_1\boxtimes E_1\simeq\widehat{\mathds{G}}_a$, and inductively $E_i\simeq E_1\boxtimes E_{i-1}$ is additive for every $i\ge2$.
Additive groups have infinite height, while the first entry is unchanged.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:HG-qF-dichotomy}
Let $Z$ be a Hodge-good smooth proper geometrically connected algebraic space of dimension $2n\ge4$ over a perfect field of characteristic $p$, with $\omega_Z\simeq\mathcal{O}_Z$.
Then
\[
  \operatorname{ht}(Z)=\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^{2n}_Z)=
  \begin{cases}
    1, & \operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_Z)=1,\\
    \infty, & \operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_Z)>1.
  \end{cases}
\]
Thus $Z$ is quasi-$F$-split if and only if it is $F$-split, equivalently if and only if $\Phi^2_Z$ has height one.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By \Cref{prop:AM-hodge-good}(1), the formal groups $\Phi^2_Z$ and $\Phi^{2n}_Z$ are smooth and one-dimensional.
Put $M=\mathbf{M}(\Phi^{2n}_Z)=\operatorname{H}^{2n}(Z,W\mathcal{O}_Z)$ (\Cref{prop:AM-cartier}).
If $Z$ is quasi-$F$-split, then $M$ is finitely generated over $W$ by \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(2), so $\Phi^{2n}_Z$ has finite height by \Cref{rem:AM-infinite-height}.
The height pattern of \Cref{cor:boxheights} then forces $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_Z)=\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^{2n}_Z)=1$.

Conversely, suppose $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_Z)=1$.
By \Cref{cor:boxheights}, the top formal group also has height one, so $F$ is bijective on $M$ and $V=pF^{-1}$.
Thus $M/VM=M/pM$, and $F$ acts nontrivially on this one-dimensional quotient.
The isomorphism $M/VM\simeq\operatorname{H}^{2n}(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)$ from \eqref{eq:rhoi} is induced by Witt restriction, which commutes with Frobenius; hence Frobenius is nonzero on top coherent cohomology.
Hence $Z$ is $F$-split by \Cref{lem:Fsplit}, and $\operatorname{ht}(Z)=1$ by \Cref{def:quasi-f-split}.
If $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^2_Z)>1$, then \Cref{cor:boxheights} gives $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^{2n}_Z)=\infty$, and the first implication shows that $Z$ is not quasi-$F$-split, so $\operatorname{ht}(Z)=\infty$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:cartier-vs-verbitsky}
The Verbitsky comparison (\Cref{prop:quotient}) uses a characteristic-zero lift and $p$-adic Hodge theory to determine $(D_{2i})_{[0,1)}$, without assuming Hodge-goodness.
The Cartier argument assumes \eqref{eq:HG}, uses no lift, and identifies the formal groups integrally, giving their heights in every even degree.
For Hodge-good reductions, the height pattern in \Cref{cor:boxheights}, together with \Cref{prop:AM-cartier,prop:WittSlope}, recovers the top-degree slope description of \Cref{cor:automatic-top-slopes}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:Witt-Euler}
Let $Z$ be a smooth proper algebraic space of dimension $d$ over a perfect field, and suppose $\operatorname{H}^j(Z,W\mathcal{O}_Z)$ is finitely generated over $W$ for every $j$.
Then
\[
  \chi(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)=E_0(Z) .
\]
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Write $M_j=\operatorname{H}^j(Z,W\mathcal{O}_Z)$ and let $V_j$ denote the Verschiebung on $M_j$, a $\sigma^{-1}$-semilinear endomorphism.
The finite length of each $\operatorname{H}^j(Z,W_r\mathcal{O}_Z)$ makes these inverse systems satisfy the Mittag--Leffler condition, so $M_j$ is computed by the inverse limit with no derived-limit term \cite[Proposition~4.5.2]{Olsson2007Crystalline}.
The exact sequence $0\toW\mathcal{O}_Z\xrightarrow{V}W\mathcal{O}_Z\to\mathcal{O}_Z\to0$ then gives, in each degree,
\[
  0\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker} V_j\longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^j(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)\longrightarrow\ker V_{j+1}\longrightarrow0 .
\]
Both $\ker V_j$ and $\operatorname{coker} V_j$ are killed by $p$, since $FV=VF=p$, and hence have finite length.
Moreover $M_j=0$ for $j>d$, and $V_0$ is injective.
Taking alternating sums of the displayed sequences, the terms $\ker V_{j+1}$ telescope and we obtain
\[
  \chi(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)=\sum_j(-1)^j\bigl(\operatorname{length}_W\operatorname{coker} V_j-\operatorname{length}_W\ker V_j\bigr) .
\]

It remains to evaluate each summand.
Let $M$ be a finitely generated $W$-module with such operators $F,V$, and write $T=M_{\mathrm{tors}}$ and $L=M/T$.
Then $V$ is injective on the free module $L$, and the snake lemma gives $\ker V_M=\ker V_T$ together with an exact sequence $0\to\operatorname{coker} V_T\to\operatorname{coker} V_M\to\operatorname{coker} V_L\to0$.
As $T$ has finite length and $V_T$ is semilinear for an automorphism of $W$, its kernel and cokernel have the same length, so the torsion cancels:
\[
  \operatorname{length}\operatorname{coker} V_M-\operatorname{length}\ker V_M=\operatorname{length}\operatorname{coker} V_L .
\]
Choose a basis of $L$ and let $A,B$ be the matrices of $F$ and $V$ in it, so that $A\,\sigma(B)=pI_r$ with $r=\operatorname{rank}_W L$.
Then
\[
  \operatorname{length}\operatorname{coker} V_L=v_p(\det B)=r-v_p(\det A)=r-t_N(M[1/p]) .
\]
By \Cref{prop:WittSlope} we have $M_j[1/p]\simeq\bigl(D_j(Z)\bigr)_{[0,1)}$, so the degree-$j$ index is exactly $\delta(M_j[1/p])=\delta_j(Z)$.
Substituting gives $\chi(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z)=E_0(Z)$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:HK-odd-low-slopes}
Let $X$ be a good reduction of a hyperk\"ahler variety. For every integer $0\le i\le\dim X-1$, we have $\delta_{2i+1}(X)=0$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
$D_{2i+1}$ is weakly admissible and $\operatorname{gr}^0(D_{2i+1})_K=\operatorname{H}^{2i+1}(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y)=0$, so $\operatorname{Fil}^1(D_{2i+1})_K=(D_{2i+1})_K$ and \Cref{lem:WA} implies that $D_{2i+1}$ has no Newton slope below one when $2i+1$ is odd.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:HK-Euler-slopes}
Let $X$ be a good reduction of dimension $2n$ with $n\ge2$. Then
\[
  E_0(X)=
  \begin{cases}
    n+1, & h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1,\\
    2,   & 1<h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)<\infty,\\
    1,   & h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=\infty .
  \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Degree zero contributes $\delta_0=1$, and all odd degrees contribute zero by \Cref{lem:HK-odd-low-slopes}.
In degree two, if $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}=h<\infty$ then the block below one has slope $1-\tfrac1h$ and multiplicity $h$, so $\delta_2=h\bigl(1-(1-\tfrac1h)\bigr)=1$; if $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}=\infty$ then $\delta_2=0$.
For $2\le i\le n$, \Cref{prop:quotient} identifies the slopes below one in $D_{2i}$ with those of $\operatorname{Sym}^iD_2$.

If $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}=1$, the only such slope is a slope-zero line, so $\delta_{2i}=1$ for every $0\le i\le n$ and $E_0=n+1$.
If $1<h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}<\infty$, every slope of $\operatorname{Sym}^iD_2$ is at least $i/2\ge1$ for $i\ge2$, so $\delta_{2i}=0$ in those degrees and $E_0=\delta_0+\delta_2=2$.
If $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}=\infty$, every degree-two slope is already at least one, so $\delta_{2i}=0$ for all $i\ge1$ and $E_0=1$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:unconditional-ordinary}
For a good reduction $X$, we have the following implications
\[
  h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1\ \Longrightarrow\  \text{ $X$ is $F$-split}\ \bigl(\Longleftrightarrow\ \operatorname{ht}(X)=1 \bigr).
\]
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Extending the perfect residue field, we may assume that it is algebraically closed.
Set $H=\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$, and let $T\subseteq H$ denote its $W$-torsion submodule.
The exact sequence
\[
  0\longrightarrowW\mathcal{O}_X\xrightarrow{\ V\ }W\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow0
\]
gives $H/VH\simeq\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=k$ in top degree, and \Cref{cor:automatic-top-slopes} together with \Cref{prop:WittSlope} shows that $H[1/p]$ is a rank-one slope-zero isocrystal.
By \cite[Theorem~4.5.12]{Olsson2007Crystalline}, $L=H/T$ is a free $W$-module of rank one; $V$ is injective on $L$ since $FV=p$.
The snake lemma applied to $0\to T\to H\to L\to0$ then gives
\[
  0\longrightarrow T/VT\longrightarrow H/VH\longrightarrow L/VL\longrightarrow0 .
\]
The last term is nonzero while the middle one has dimension $1$, so $T/VT=0$; as $H$, and hence $T$, is $V$-adically separated \cite[Corollary~4.5.6]{Olsson2007Crystalline}, $T=VT$ forces $T=0$.
Thus $H$ is free of rank one.

Because $H[1/p]$ has slope zero, $F$ is bijective on it, and $FV=p$ forces $VH=pH$; hence $F$ is a unit on $H$ and acts nontrivially on $H/VH=\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
Since $\omega_X\simeq\mathcal{O}_X$ by \Cref{prop:canonical-good}, \Cref{lem:Fsplit} shows that $X$ is Frobenius split.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:all-good-dichotomy}
Let $X$ be a good reduction of a projective irreducible hyperk\"ahler variety of dimension $2n\ge4$, in the setting of \Cref{subsec:automatic}.
The smooth proper model and its special fibre may be algebraic spaces.
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $X$ is quasi-$F$-split;
\item $X$ is Frobenius split;
\item $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$;
\item $\operatorname{H}^j(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is finitely generated over $W$ for every $j$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently
\[
  \operatorname{ht}(X)=
  \begin{cases}
    1, & h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1,\\
    \infty, & h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1.
  \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Condition (i) implies (iv) by \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(2).
If (iv) holds, then \Cref{prop:Witt-Euler} and $\chi(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=n+1$ (\Cref{prop:canonical-good}) give $E_0(X)=n+1$; since $n+1\ge3$, the two non-ordinary values $2$ and $1$ allowed by \Cref{prop:HK-Euler-slopes} are impossible, so $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$ and (iv) implies (iii).
\Cref{prop:unconditional-ordinary} gives (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii), and (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(1).

For the last assertion, if $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$ then $\operatorname{ht}(X)=1$ by \Cref{prop:unconditional-ordinary}.
If $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$ then $X$ fails (iii), hence also (i), and $\operatorname{ht}(X)=\infty$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:iii-equiv}, condition (iii) of \Cref{thm:main-all-good} is equivalent to $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$, so the statement is exactly \Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-supersingularity}
The dichotomy does not imply full supersingularity: it does not force all slopes of $\operatorname{H}^{2i}_{\operatorname{crys}}$ to equal $i$ when $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$.
The argument also does not identify which Witt-vector cohomology group fails to be finitely generated; \Cref{prop:top-witt-criterion} identifies the top degree when $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:hodge-witt-dichotomy}
If a good reduction $X$ of dimension $2n\ge4$ has $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$, then there is some $j$ for which $\operatorname{H}^j(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is not finitely generated over $W$.
In particular, $X$ is not Hodge--Witt.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:hilb2}
By \Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy} and \Cref{ex:hilb,ex:kummer}, the quasi-$F$-splitting height of either series can be read off from the surface which it is built on:
\[
  \begin{aligned}
    \operatorname{ht}\bigl(S^{[n]}\bigr)
      &=\begin{cases}
          1,      & S\text{ ordinary},\\
          \infty, & S\text{ non-ordinary},
        \end{cases}\\
    \operatorname{ht}\bigl(K_n(A)\bigr)
      &=\begin{cases}
          1,      & A\text{ ordinary},\\
          \infty, & A\text{ non-ordinary}.
        \end{cases}
  \end{aligned}
\]
This is consistent with Yobuko's direct computation that $S^{[n]}$ with $n\ge2$ is quasi-$F$-split only if $S$ is Frobenius split \cite[Theorem~5.6]{Yobuko2023}.
In particular, if $S$ is a non-ordinary $K3$ surface, or $A$ a non-ordinary abelian surface, of finite formal Brauer height $h>1$, then $S^{[n]}$ and $K_n(A)$ are neither quasi-$F$-split nor Hodge--Witt; \Cref{cor:generalized Kummer and Hilbert scheme no fg} below makes this precise.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:ordinary-sheaf-moduli-F-split}
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$. Let $Z$ be a $K3$ or abelian surface. In each case let $v=(r,c_1,s)$ be an algebraic Mukai vector on the indicated surface $Z$, with $\langle v,v\rangle=c_1^2-2rs$, and let $H$ be an ample polarization general for $v$. Write $M_H(Z,v)$ for the moduli space of Gieseker-stable sheaves on $Z$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item If $S/k$ is an ordinary $K3$ surface and $v$ is primitive with $r>0$ and $\langle v,v\rangle>0$, then $M_H(S,v)$ is $F$-split.
\item If $A/k$ is an ordinary abelian surface and $v$ is primitive with $r>0$ and $\langle v,v\rangle=2n+2$ for $n\ge2$ and $p\nmid n+1$, then both the Albanese fibre $K_H(A,v)$ and $M_H(A,v)$ are $F$-split.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let $Z=S$ in case \textup{(a)} and $Z=A$ in case \textup{(b)}. By \Cref{lem:ordinary-surface-slopes}, $(D_2(Z))_{[0,1)}$ is a line of slope zero. Consider the crystalline Mukai isocrystal
\[
  \widetilde D(Z)=D_0(Z)(-1)\oplus D_2(Z)\oplus D_4(Z)(1)
\]
whose outer summands have slope one, as does $K_0 v$. The Mukai pairing takes values in $K_0(-2)$, of slope two. A slope-$\lambda$ subobject with $\lambda<1$ therefore pairs trivially with $K_0 v$, since their tensor product has slope $\lambda+1<2$. Thus $(v^\perp)_{[0,1)}=(D_2(Z))_{[0,1)}$ is a line of slope zero.

In case \textup{(a)}, \cite[Proposition~4.4 and its proof]{FuLi2021} gives a smooth projective mixed-characteristic lift of $M_H(S,v)$ with hyperk\"ahler geometric generic fibre and an isomorphism $D_2(M_H(S,v))\simeq v^\perp$ of isocrystals. Hence $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(M_H(S,v))=1$, so \Cref{prop:unconditional-ordinary} gives the assertion. The same argument applies to $K_H(A,v)$ by \cite[Proposition~6.9 and its proof]{FuLi2021}, proving the first assertion of \textup{(b)}. Here we use the local form of \Cref{prop:unconditional-ordinary}: its proof also applies to these complete mixed-characteristic lifts with perfect residue field.

Finally, $A\times\widehat A$ is ordinary and hence $F$-split. The isotrivialization of the Albanese map in \cite[diagram~(50)]{FuLi2021} gives a finite \'etale cover
\[
  K_H(A,v)\times A\times\widehat A\longrightarrow M_H(A,v)
\]
of degree $(n+1)^8$, prime to $p$. Its source is $F$-split, and the normalized trace descends a Frobenius splitting to $M_H(A,v)$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:primitive}
A smooth proper algebraic space $X$ over $k$ is \emph{primitive} if $h^{0,1}(X)=\dim_k\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:qF-Picard}
If a good reduction $X$ of dimension $2n\ge4$ is quasi-$F$-split, then $X$ is primitive.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By \Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy}, $X$ is Frobenius split, so Frobenius is injective on $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.
But it is nilpotent there by \Cref{prop:automatic-picard} and hence $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:top-witt-criterion}
Let $X$ be a good reduction of dimension $2n\ge4$, in the setting of \Cref{subsec:automatic}, and suppose $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
Then $X$ is quasi-$F$-split if and only if $\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is finitely generated over $W$. Moreover, we have
\[ \operatorname{ht}(X) = \operatorname{ht}(\Phi^{2n}_X) \in \{ 1, \infty \}.\]
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
If $X$ is quasi-$F$-split, then $\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is finitely generated by \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(2); this direction uses no hypothesis on $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$.

Since $\omega_X\simeq\mathcal{O}_X$ and $X$ is smooth proper and geometrically connected (\Cref{prop:canonical-good}), Serre duality gives
\[
  \operatorname{H}^{2n-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\simeq\operatorname{H}^1(X,\omega_X)^{\vee}=\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)^{\vee}=0,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\simeq\operatorname{H}^0(X,\omega_X)^{\vee}=k .
\]
Conversely, suppose $X$ is not quasi-$F$-split, so that $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$ by \Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy}.
For $m\geq 2$ the Witt sheaves sit in exact sequences
\[
  0\longrightarrow\mathcal{O}_X\xrightarrow{\ V^{m-1}\ }W_m\mathcal{O}_X
   \xrightarrow{\ R\ }W_{m-1}\mathcal{O}_X\longrightarrow0 .
\]
Induction on $m$ gives $\operatorname{H}^{2n-1}(X,W_m\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ for all $m\geq 1$, the long exact sequence squeezing this group between $\operatorname{H}^{2n-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ and $\operatorname{H}^{2n-1}(X,W_{m-1}\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
The same sequences therefore give short exact sequences
\[
  0\longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W_m\mathcal{O}_X)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W_{m-1}\mathcal{O}_X)\longrightarrow0,
\]
surjective on the right because $\operatorname{H}^{2n+1}$ vanishes.
Hence
\[
  \operatorname{length}_W\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W_m\mathcal{O}_X)=m
\]
for every $m$.
The transition maps $R$ are surjective, so the inverse limit $\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ surjects onto each $\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W_m\mathcal{O}_X)$ and has infinite length.

On the other hand $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$ forces $(D_{2n})_{[0,1)}=0$ by \Cref{cor:automatic-top-slopes}, so \( \operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)[1/p]=0\) by \Cref{prop:WittSlope}.
A finitely generated torsion $W$-module has finite length, so $\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is not finitely generated.

Finally, the vanishing of $\operatorname{H}^{2n-1}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ and the isomorphism
$\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,\mathcal{O}_X)\simeqk$ show that $\Phi_X^{2n}$ is a smooth
one-dimensional formal group by \Cref{lem:AM-prorepresentable}.
By \Cref{cor:automatic-top-slopes}, the slope-$[0,1)$ part of $D_{2n}$
is a line of slope zero when $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)=1$, and vanishes when
$h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$.
Thus \Cref{rem:AM-slope-convention} gives $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi_X^{2n})=1$ in the
first case and $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi_X^{2n})=\infty$ in the second.
These are exactly the two values of $\operatorname{ht}(X)$ in
\Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:generalized Kummer and Hilbert scheme no fg}
Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p$, let $n\ge2$, and let $X$ be either
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item the Hilbert scheme $X=S^{[n]}$ of $n$ points on a $K3$ surface $S$ over $k$, with $p >2$; or
\item the generalised Kummer variety $X=K_n(A)$ attached to an abelian surface $A$ over $k$, with $p>2$ and $p\nmid n+1$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $X$ is smooth of dimension $2n\ge4$ and is a good reduction of a hyperk\"ahler variety.
If the underlying surface $S$, respectively $A$, is not ordinary, or equivalently if $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$, then $X$ is not quasi-$F$-split and
\[
  \operatorname{length}_W\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)=\infty .
\]
In particular $\operatorname{H}^{2n}(X,W\mathcal{O}_X)$ is a $W$-torsion module that is not finitely generated over $W$.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
In both cases $X$ is a smooth good reduction of a hyperk\"ahler variety of dimension $2n\ge4$ by the existence of algebraic lifting over $W(k)$.
\Cref{prop:h1-vanishing-small-e} gives $\operatorname{H}^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$.
The slope-$[0,1)$ part of $D_2$ is that of the underlying surface (\Cref{ex:hilb,ex:kummer}), so $h_2^{\operatorname{crys}}(X)>1$ precisely when that surface is non-ordinary; then $X$ is not quasi-$F$-split by \Cref{thm:all-good-dichotomy}, and \Cref{prop:top-witt-criterion} applies.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:HG-open}
Assume $d=2n$.
Then $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$ is open in $S$, and its formation commutes with base change on $S$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The assertion is immediate for $n=0$, so assume $n\ge1$.
Hodge-goodness of $\mathcal{X}_{\bar s}$ is equivalent to that of $\mathcal{X}_s$, as \eqref{eq:HG} may be tested after the flat base change $\kappa(s)\to\kappa(\bar{s})$, and it is a condition on fibres; since $\mathcal{X}\times_SS_{\mathrm{red}}\to S_{\mathrm{red}}$ has the same fibres as $f$, we may assume $S$ reduced.
Let $s_0\in S^{\operatorname{HG}}$; we produce an open neighbourhood of $s_0$ inside $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$.

Since $f$ is flat and proper, $s\mapsto\chi(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$ is locally constant, and \eqref{eq:HG} gives $\chi(\mathcal{X}_{s_0},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_{s_0}})=n+1$; shrink $S$ so that $\chi(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})=n+1$ for every $s$.
By the semicontinuity theorem each function $s\mapsto h^q(s)\coloneqq\dim_{\kappa(s)}\operatorname{H}^q(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$ is upper semicontinuous, so
\[
  V=\bigl\{\,s\in S \mid h^q(s)\le h^q(s_0)\ \text{for all } q\,\bigr\}
\]
is open and contains $s_0$.
On $V$ we have $h^q(s)=0$ for odd $q$ and $h^{2i}(s)\le1$ for $0\le i\le n$, whence
\[
  n+1=\chi(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})=\sum_{i=0}^{n}h^{2i}(s)\le n+1 .
\]
Equality forces $h^{2i}(s)=1$ for every $i$ and every $s\in V$.
Thus all the functions $h^q$ are constant on $V$; as $V$ is reduced, Grauert's theorem makes each $R^qf_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}|_V$ locally free of that rank with formation commuting with arbitrary base change.
In particular $R^{2i}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}|_V$ is invertible for $0\le i\le n$.

The top cup-power map
\[
  (R^2f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}|_V)^{\otimes n}
     \longrightarrow R^{2n}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}|_V
\]
is a map of line bundles, so its non-vanishing locus is open and contains $s_0$.
On each fibre in this locus, a generator $\eta\in\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$ satisfies $\eta^n\ne0$, hence $\eta^i\ne0$ for every $0\le i\le n$.
These powers generate the one-dimensional even cohomology groups, proving \eqref{eq:HG} there.
The same fibrewise description proves compatibility with base change.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:Fsplit-open}
The locus $S^{\operatorname{Fs}}$ is open in $S$, and equals $\{\,s\in S \mid \operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s})=1\,\}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Geometric connectedness gives $f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}=\mathcal{O}_S$.
Relative Serre duality and \eqref{eq:family-setup} therefore make $L=R^df_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$ invertible, with formation commuting with arbitrary base change and $L\otimes\kappa(s)=\operatorname{H}^d(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$.
The relative Frobenius $\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}\times_{S,F_S}S$ induces an $\mathcal{O}_S$-linear map $F_S^*L\to L$ whose fibre at $s$ is the absolute Frobenius on $\operatorname{H}^d(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$.
A map of invertible sheaves is a section of an invertible sheaf, so its non-vanishing locus is open.
Non-vanishing can be tested after passage to $\kappa(\bar s)$, where \Cref{lem:Fsplit,def:quasi-f-split} identify it with $F$-splitting and with height one.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:relative-AM-family}
Assume \eqref{eq:family-h01}.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $R^{d-1}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}=0$, and $R^df_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$ is an invertible $\mathcal{O}_S$-module whose formation commutes with arbitrary base change.
\item The relative Artin--Mazur functor $\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}/S}$ is prorepresentable by a smooth one-dimensional formal group $G$ over $S$, with $\operatorname{Lie}(G)\simeq R^df_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $G\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\simeq\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}_s}$ for every $s\in S$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
(1) Each fibre is smooth proper and geometrically connected with $\omega_{\mathcal{X}_s}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s}$, so Serre duality gives
\[
  \operatorname{H}^{d-1}(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})\simeq\operatorname{H}^{1}(\mathcal{X}_s,\omega_{\mathcal{X}_s})^{\vee}
  =\operatorname{H}^{1}(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})^{\vee}=0
\]
by \eqref{eq:family-h01}.
Cohomology and base change gives $R^{d-1}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}\otimes\kappa(s)=0$ for every $s$ and hence $R^{d-1}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}=0$ by Nakayama.
The assertion about $R^df_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$ was proved in \Cref{lem:Fsplit-open}.

(2) The fibrewise assertion is \Cref{lem:AM-prorepresentable} applied with $q=d$: the hypothesis $\operatorname{H}^{d-1}(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})=0$ of part (2) there holds by (1), the obstruction group $\operatorname{H}^{d+1}(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$ vanishes for dimensional reasons, and the tangent space $\operatorname{H}^d(\mathcal{X}_s,\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}_s})$ is one-dimensional.
The relative statement is the same criterion of \cite[\S II]{ArtinMazur1977} applied to $f$: by (1) the sheaf $R^{d-1}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$ vanishes and $R^{d+1}f_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}=0$, so $\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}/S}$ is prorepresentable and formally smooth over $S$ with tangent sheaf $R^df_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$, which is invertible; and its formation commutes with base change $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\to S$ because that of $R^df_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}$ does.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:height-semicontinuity}
Assume \eqref{eq:family-h01}.
The function $s\mapsto\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}_s})$ is upper semicontinuous: for every $h\ge1$, the locus $\{\,s\in S:\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}_s})\ge h\,\}$ is closed.
In particular, $S^{\operatorname{fin}}$ is open.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Let $G$ be the formal group of \Cref{lem:relative-AM-family}(2).
The question is local on $S$, so we may assume that $G$ admits a coordinate, that is $G\simeq\mathcal{O}_S[[t]]$ as a formal scheme, with a one-dimensional formal group law over $\Gamma(S,\mathcal{O}_S)$.
Write its multiplication-by-$p$ endomorphism as
\[
  [p]_G(t)=\sum_{i\ge1}a_it^{i},\qquad a_i\in\Gamma(S,\mathcal{O}_S).
\]
Its formation commutes with base change, so $[p]_{G_s}(t)=\sum_i a_i(s)t^i$ for every $s$.
Over a field of characteristic $p$ a one-dimensional formal group has height at least $h$ precisely when its $p$-series lies in $\kappa(s)[[t^{p^{h}}]]$, that is, precisely when $a_i(s)=0$ for every $i<p^{h}$.
Hence
\[
  \{~ s \mid \operatorname{ht}(\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}_s})\ge h~\}=\bigcap_{i<p^{h}}\{\,s \mid a_i(s)=0\,\}
\]
is closed, and its complement $\{\operatorname{ht}\le h-1\}$ is open.
Finally $S^{\operatorname{fin}}=\bigcup_{h\ge1}\{\operatorname{ht}\le h\}$ is a union of open subsets.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:qF-in-fin}
Assume \eqref{eq:family-h01}.
Then $S^{\operatorname{qF}}\subseteq S^{\operatorname{fin}}$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Let $s\in S^{\operatorname{qF}}$ and work over the perfect field $\kappa(\bar{s})$.
By \Cref{lem:relative-AM-family}(2) the functor $\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}_{\bar s}}$ is a smooth one-dimensional formal group, and by \eqref{eq:family-h01} and Serre duality the hypotheses of \Cref{thm:nakkajima-inequality} hold in degree $q=d$: the tangent space $\operatorname{H}^d(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s},\mathcal{O})$ is $\kappa(\bar{s})$, the obstruction group $\operatorname{H}^{d+1}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s},\mathcal{O})$ vanishes, and the Bockstein maps vanish because their source $\operatorname{H}^{d-1}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s},\mathcal{O})$ is zero.
That theorem gives $\operatorname{ht}(\Phi^d_{\mathcal{X}_{\bar s}})\le\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s})<\infty$, so $s\in S^{\operatorname{fin}}$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:openness-gap}
The reverse inclusion $S^{\operatorname{fin}}\subseteq S^{\operatorname{qF}}$ is not established here in general.
The next result gives equality on the Hodge-good locus in dimension at least four.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:dichotomy in a family}
Assume $d=2n\ge4$.
Then
\[
  S^{\operatorname{Fs}}\cap S^{\operatorname{HG}}
    =S^{\operatorname{qF}}\cap S^{\operatorname{HG}}
    =S^{\operatorname{fin}}\cap S^{\operatorname{HG}}
\]
is open in $S$.
The height $\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s})$ is $1$ on this common locus and $\infty$ on its complement in $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
For $s\in S^{\operatorname{HG}}$, the geometric fibre $\mathcal{X}_{\bar s}$ is Hodge-good, smooth proper and geometrically connected, with trivial canonical bundle and dimension $2n\ge4$.
Moreover, \eqref{eq:family-h01} holds on $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$ by \eqref{eq:HG}, so its top Artin--Mazur group is defined by \Cref{lem:relative-AM-family}.
Applying \Cref{cor:HG-qF-dichotomy} over $\kappa(\bar s)$ gives the equalities and the height assertion.
Openness follows from \Cref{lem:HG-open,lem:Fsplit-open}.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:generic-dichotomy}
Assume $d=2n\ge4$, $S$ is irreducible with generic point $\eta$, $S^{\operatorname{HG}}\ne\emptyset$, and \eqref{eq:family-h01} holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $S^{\operatorname{fin}}\ne\emptyset$ if and only if $S^{\operatorname{qF}}\ne\emptyset$, if and only if the geometric generic fibre is $F$-split.
\item If the geometric generic fibre is not $F$-split, then $S^{\operatorname{fin}}=S^{\operatorname{qF}}=\emptyset$ and $\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s})=\infty$ for every $s\in S$.
\item The dichotomy $\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{X}_{\bar s})\in\{1,\infty\}$ holds on the dense open subset $S^{\operatorname{HG}}\cup S^{\operatorname{Fs}}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
(i) If $S^{\operatorname{fin}}\ne\emptyset$, both $S^{\operatorname{fin}}$ and $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$ are nonempty open subsets by \Cref{prop:height-semicontinuity,lem:HG-open}.
They contain $\eta$, so \Cref{thm:dichotomy in a family} gives $\eta\in S^{\operatorname{Fs}}$.
The other implications follow from $S^{\operatorname{Fs}}\subseteq S^{\operatorname{qF}}\subseteq S^{\operatorname{fin}}$, using \Cref{lem:basic-properties}(1) and \Cref{prop:qF-in-fin}.

(ii) By (i), $S^{\operatorname{fin}}=S^{\operatorname{qF}}=\emptyset$, so every geometric fibre has infinite quasi-$F$-split height by definition.

(iii) Apply \Cref{thm:dichotomy in a family} on $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$ and \Cref{lem:Fsplit-open} on $S^{\operatorname{Fs}}$.
Their union is open and contains the nonempty open subset $S^{\operatorname{HG}}$, hence is dense in the irreducible base $S$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:relative-W2-lifting}
Let $B$ be a smooth finite-type $k$-scheme and let $g\colon\mathcal{Y}\to B$ be smooth and proper.
Assume that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ct2}
  b\longmapsto\dim_{\kappa(b)}\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{Y}_b,T_{\mathcal{Y}_b})
  \tag{$\textup{ct}_2$}
\end{equation}
is locally constant on the set of closed points of $B$.
Then $R^2g_*T_{\mathcal{Y}/B}$ is locally free and its formation commutes with arbitrary base change, and for every affine open $U\subseteq B$ and every smooth affine $W_2(k)$-lifting $\widetilde U$ of $U$ there is a class
\[
  o\in\Gamma\bigl(U,R^2g_*T_{\mathcal{Y}/B}\bigr)
\]
with the following two properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $o=0$ if and only if $\mathcal{Y}_U$ admits a smooth proper lifting over $\widetilde U$.
\item For every closed point $b\in U$, the value $o(b)$ is the obstruction to lifting $\mathcal{Y}_b$ over $W_2(\kappa(b))$.
  Thus the non-liftable closed fibres are the closed points of an open subset of $U$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if the closed fibres over a dense open subset of $B$ lift to $W_2(\kappa(b))$, then locally on $B$ the morphism $g$ admits a smooth proper lifting over a smooth $W_2(k)$-lifting of its base.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The sheaf $T_{\mathcal{Y}/B}$ is locally free and $B$-flat, so $b\mapsto\dim\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{Y}_b,T_{\mathcal{Y}_b})$ is upper semicontinuous on $B$.
A finite-type $k$-scheme is Jacobson, so a closed subset meeting no closed point is empty; hence local constancy on closed points forces local constancy on $B$.

Fix $b\in B$ and put $A=\mathcal{O}_{B,b}$, a regular local domain.
By properness $Rg_*T_{\mathcal{Y}/B}$ is a perfect complex whose formation commutes with derived base change; choose a minimal finite free model $P^\bullet$ of it over $A$, so that the differentials of $P^\bullet$ have entries in the maximal ideal and $\dim\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{Y}_b,T_{\mathcal{Y}_b})=\operatorname{rank} P^2$.
By the local constancy just established the same number computes the second cohomology of $P^\bullet$ at the generic point of $\operatorname{Spec} A$, so the two differentials adjacent to degree two vanish there; as $A$ is a domain and $P^\bullet$ is free, they vanish.
Hence $\operatorname{H}^2(P^\bullet)=P^2$, and $R^2g_*T_{\mathcal{Y}/B}$ is locally free with formation commuting with arbitrary base change.

Let $U\subseteq B$ be an affine open subset and $\widetilde U$ a smooth affine $W_2(k)$-lifting of $U$, which exists by lifting an \'etale coordinate presentation.
Flatness of $\widetilde U$ over $W_2(k)$ identifies the square-zero ideal $p\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde U}$ with $\mathcal{O}_U$ through multiplication by $p$, so the obstruction to extending $\mathcal{Y}_U\to U$ to a flat lifting over $\widetilde U$ is a class
\[
  o\in\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{Y}_U}\bigl(\Omega^1_{\mathcal{Y}_U/U},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{Y}_U}\bigr)
   =\operatorname{H}^2\bigl(\mathcal{Y}_U,T_{\mathcal{Y}_U/U}\bigr)
   =\Gamma\bigl(U,R^2g_*T_{\mathcal{Y}/B}\bigr),
\]
the first equality because smoothness identifies the relative cotangent complex with $\Omega^1_{\mathcal{Y}_U/U}$; the class vanishes if and only if such a lifting exists \cite[Chapter~III, \S2.1]{Illusie1971}.
A flat lifting is automatically smooth and proper, both properties persisting across a nilpotent thickening of the base, so this is \textup{(i)}.

For \textup{(ii)}, smoothness of $\widetilde U$ over $W_2(k)$ lifts a closed point $b\in U$ to a $W_2(\kappa(b))$-point of $\widetilde U$, the residue field $\kappa(b)$ being finite over $k$ and hence perfect.
By the base-change property established above, together with naturality of the obstruction along that morphism of square-zero extensions, the value $o(b)$ is the obstruction to lifting $\mathcal{Y}_b$ over $W_2(\kappa(b))$.
The non-vanishing locus of a section of a locally free sheaf is open, which gives the last assertion of \textup{(ii)}.

If the closed fibres lift over a dense open subset $V\subseteq B$, then $o$ vanishes at every closed point of $U\cap V$.
Since $B$ is reduced and Jacobson, $o$ vanishes on $U\cap V$, hence on $U$.
Thus $o=0$ and \textup{(i)} applies.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:relative-W2-from-one-fibre}
Under the hypotheses of \Cref{lem:relative-W2-lifting}, suppose $B$ is connected and one geometric fibre is connected, has trivial canonical bundle, has $E_1$-degeneration, and has torsion-free crystalline cohomology in every degree.
Then, locally on $B$, the morphism $g$ admits a smooth proper lifting over a smooth $W_2(k)$-lifting of its base.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Let $Y_0$ be the specified geometric fibre and write $d=\dim Y_0$.
Smooth proper base change makes all geometric fibres connected and their Betti numbers $b_j$ constant.
The assumptions on $Y_0$ give $\sum_{a+b=j}h^{a,b}(Y_0)=b_j$ for every $j$.
By upper semicontinuity there is an open neighbourhood $V$ of its image on which $h^{a,b}(\mathcal{Y}_{\bar t})\le h^{a,b}(Y_0)$ for all $a,b$.
For $t\in V$,
\[
 b_j\le\dim\operatorname{H}^j_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{Y}_{\bar t})
     \le\sum_{a+b=j}h^{a,b}(\mathcal{Y}_{\bar t})\le b_j.
\]
The first inequality follows from the crystalline universal-coefficient sequence.
Equality throughout gives constant Hodge numbers on $V$, $E_1$-degeneration, and torsion-free crystalline cohomology in every degree.
In particular $g_*\omega_{\mathcal{Y}_V/V}$ is a line bundle and commutes with base change.
Its evaluation map is an isomorphism on $Y_0$.
The locus in $\mathcal{Y}_V$ where it is not an isomorphism is closed and has closed image in $V$ by properness.
Removing that image leaves an open neighbourhood of the image of $Y_0$ on which every fibre has trivial canonical bundle.
By \cite[Theorem~7.18]{BrantnerTaelman2025}, all closed fibres over this open subset lift to $W_2$.
Since $B$ is smooth and connected, it is integral, so this open subset is dense and \Cref{lem:relative-W2-lifting} applies.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:HG-locally-constant}
Let $B$ be a smooth connected finite-type $k$-scheme and let $g\colon\mathcal{Y}\to B$ be smooth proper of relative dimension $2n$, with $n\ge1$.
Suppose that, locally on $B$, the morphism $g$ admits a smooth lifting over a smooth $W_2(k)$-lifting of its base.
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item For $a+b<p$, the sheaves $R^bg_*\Omega^a_{\mathcal{Y}/B}$ are locally free and commute with arbitrary base change.
  For $1\le r\le n$ with $2r<p$, both maps
\[
    (R^2g_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{Y}})^{\otimes r}\longrightarrow R^{2r}g_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{Y}},
    \qquad
    (g_*\Omega^2_{\mathcal{Y}/B})^{\otimes r}\longrightarrow g_*\Omega^{2r}_{\mathcal{Y}/B}
  \]
  have locally constant rank.
  \item If $2n<p$, the local-freeness and base-change assertions hold for all $a,b$, and the locus of Hodge-good geometric fibres is open and closed.
  \item Suppose every geometric fibre has trivial canonical bundle.
    If $n\le p$, all $R^qg_*\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{Y}}$ are locally free and commute with arbitrary base change.
    If $n<p$, the locus of Hodge-good geometric fibres is either empty or all of $B$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Work over an affine open $U\subseteq B$ carrying a lifting $\widetilde{\mathcal{Y}}\to\widetilde U$ of $\mathcal{Y}_U\to U$ with $\widetilde U$ smooth over $W_2(k)$.
We first obtain the low-degree Deligne--Illusie comparison.
Smoothness of $\widetilde U$ provides a lift of the absolute Frobenius of $U$, semilinear for the Witt Frobenius; base changing $\widetilde{\mathcal{Y}}$ along it lifts the Frobenius twist $\mathcal{Y}'=\mathcal{Y}_U\times_{U,F_U}U$.
It is this lifting of $\mathcal{Y}'$, and not a lifting of individual fibres, that the relative form of the Deligne--Illusie theorem consumes \cite[Corollary~3.7(a), Remark~4.1.6]{DeligneIllusie1987}.
Without any dimension bound, the resulting decomposition is
\[
  \phi\colon\bigoplus_{0\le a<p}\Omega^a_{\mathcal{Y}'/U}[-a]
  \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\tau_{<p}F_*\Omega^\bullet_{\mathcal{Y}_U/U}
  \qquad\text{in }D(\mathcal{Y}'),
\]
$F$ denoting the relative Frobenius, and $\phi$ may be chosen compatibly with products in total form degree less than $p$, that is $\phi_{a+b}(u\wedge v)=\phi_a(u)\phi_b(v)$ for $a+b<p$: one takes $\phi_1$, forms its tensor powers, antisymmetrises by $1/a!$, which is legitimate exactly in the range $a<p$, and composes with the multiplication of the de Rham complex \cite[proof of Theorem~2.1(a) and Corollary~3.7(a)]{DeligneIllusie1987}.
By \cite[Corollary~4.1.4]{DeligneIllusie1987} the sheaves $E^{a,b}=R^bg_*\Omega^a_{\mathcal{Y}_U/U}$ and $D^m=R^mg_*\Omega^\bullet_{\mathcal{Y}_U/U}$ are locally free and commute with arbitrary base change for $a+b<p$ and $m<p$, respectively, and the relative Hodge spectral sequence degenerates in these total degrees.
Since the omitted truncation has hypercohomology only in degrees at least $p$, $\phi$ induces isomorphisms \footnote{These need not preserve the Hodge filtration.}
\[
  \theta_m\colon F_U^*\Bigl(\bigoplus_a E^{a,m-a}\Bigr)
  \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }D^m,\qquad m<p.
\]

For $1\le r\le n$ with $2r<p$, let $u_r\colon(D^2)^{\otimes r}\to D^{2r}$ be the cup product of relative de Rham cohomology.
It is a filtered map of vector bundles for the Hodge filtration, whose associated graded $v_r$ is the direct sum, over the total form degree, of the Hodge cup products on $\bigl(\bigoplus_{a=0}^2E^{a,2-a}\bigr)^{\otimes r}$.
Every product occurring here has total form degree at most $2r<p$, so multiplicativity of $\phi$ gives $u_r\circ\theta_2^{\otimes r}=\theta_{2r}\circ F_U^*v_r$.

To show that each graded block of $v_r$ has locally constant rank, fix $b\in U$ and put $A=\mathcal{O}_{U,b}$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.
Over $A$, write $u\colon E\to G$ for $u_r$ and $v=\operatorname{gr} u$.
The Hodge filtrations split because their graded pieces are free, so we may write
\[
  E=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{2r}E_i,\qquad
  G=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{2r}G_i,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Fil}^iE=\bigoplus_{j\ge i}E_j,\quad
  \operatorname{Fil}^iG=\bigoplus_{j\ge i}G_j,
\]
where $E_i$ and $G_i$ identify with the graded pieces.
Choose bases ordered by increasing $i$.
Since $u(\operatorname{Fil}^iE)\subseteq\operatorname{Fil}^iG$, its component $E_i\to G_j$ vanishes for $j<i$.
Thus, writing $M_i$ for the matrix of $v_i\colon E_i\to G_i$, we have
\[
  M_u=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    M_0&0&\cdots&0\\
    *&M_1&\ddots&\vdots\\
    \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\
    *&\cdots&*&M_{2r}
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  M_v=
  \begin{pmatrix}
